Q: How do I get typing to work on generic class when creating a property with a function? A:

So, @builtins.property doesn't work like that in the sense that you can't def f(...) -> property to get static typing to work. In theory, it should, as @property is a class at runtime and is a perfectly valid type annotation. However, @property is heavily special-cased in static type checkers to allow the standard Python syntax @property...@...setter...@...deleter.

Yes, you would need a descriptor. Based on your given implementation, I would do something like this (mypy, pyright, pyrefly):

from typing import Protocol, Self, overload

# Minimal interface eyeballed from `builtins.property`. See
# https://github.com/python/typeshed/blob/240fd757ebd7ad4018ff8fef2c43a3748d31458b/stdlib/builtins.pyi#L1540
class Property(Protocol):
    @overload
    def __get__(self, instance: None, owner: type, /) -> Self: ...
    @overload
    def __get__[V](self, instance: Custom[V], owner: type | None = None, /) -> V: ...
    def __set__[V](self, instance: Custom[V], value: V, /) -> None: ...

def create_value_property(name: str) -> Property:
    def get(self: object) -> object: ...
    def set(self: object, value: object) -> None: ...
    return property(get, set)

class Custom[V]:
    def __init__(self, val1: V, val2: V, val3: V) -> None: ...

    val1: Property = create_value_property('val1')
    val2: Property = create_value_property('val2')
    val3: Property = create_value_property('val3')

custom = Custom[int](1,1,1)
a = custom.val1
custom.val1 = 2
custom.val2 = 3
custom.val3 = 4

reveal_type(a)  # Revealed type is "int"

Stronger guarantees using type annotations in def create_value_property are generally not possible since you're using getattr() and setattr(), although you can use something other than object (e.g. set[V](self: Custom[V], value: V) if you need to access self.event_handler).

With some additional constraints,

Can I instead do away with the create_value_property function and implement the functionality in Property so that I can do something in Custom like val1 = Property() so that I don't have to explicitly pass the variable name? Then make it generic enough so I can use property within any class that implements event_handler?

you can do this (see godbolt for runtime):

from typing import Protocol, Self, overload

class EventHandler:
    def post_event(self, event: str):
        print(event)

class SupportsEventHandler(Protocol):
    event_handler: EventHandler

class Property[V]:
    _name: str
    def __set_name__(self, owner: type[SupportsEventHandler], name: str, /) -> None:
        self._name = name

    @overload
    def __get__(self, instance: None, owner: type, /) -> Self: ...
    @overload
    def __get__(self, instance: SupportsEventHandler, owner: type | None = None, /) -> V: ...
    def __get__(self, instance: SupportsEventHandler | None, owner: type | None = None, /) -> Self | V:
        if instance is None:
            return self
        return getattr(instance, f"_{self._name}")

    def __set__(self, instance: SupportsEventHandler, value: V, /) -> None:
        prev_value = getattr(instance, f"_{self._name}")
        if value == prev_value:
            return
        setattr(instance, f"_{self._name}", value)
        instance.event_handler.post_event(f"{self._name} value changed: {value}")

class Custom[V]:
    def __init__(self, val1: V, val2: V, val3: V) -> None:
        self._val1 = val1
        self._val2 = val2
        self._val3 = val3
        self.event_handler: EventHandler = EventHandler()

    val1 = Property[V]()
    val2 = Property[V]()
    val3 = Property[V]()

custom = Custom[int](1,1,1)
a = custom.val1
custom.val1 = 1
custom.val2 = 2
custom.val3 = "asdfjkl"  # Error: Expected "int", got "str"

reveal_type(a)  # Revealed type is "int"

val2 value changed: 2
val3 value changed: asdfjkl

This is slightly clunkier in the sense that we now have to explicitly parameterise Property with [V]. While it is type-safe, you won't get type errors until you read or write the attribute instead.

Q: gganimate::animate() warns "font family not found in Windows font database" even when using ragg A:

The root cause is that {gganimate} and {showtext} use incompatible font rendering paths, and font_add_google() doesn't make fonts visible to the component that needs them.

{showtext} works by hooking into the graphics device at render time and substituting its own font rendering. This works fine for static plots, but animate() with device = "ragg_png" opens a fresh {ragg} device for each frame in a separate rendering pass. Moreover, {ragg} has its own font system ({systemfonts}) that operates independently of {showtext}. When both are active they conflict.

font_add_google() registers fonts in {sysfonts}'s internal registry but it doesn't install them to the Windows font database or to {systemfonts}. So when {gganimate} renders frames through ragg_png, the fonts aren't where {ragg} looks.

{gganimate} builds each frame as a ggplot grob and renders it via the device specified in animate(). Even with device = "ragg_png", grid measures text layout before the device renders; C_textBounds and C_stringMetric are grid's internal C-level calls for computing text dimensions, and on Windows they go through GDI (Graphics Device Interface) for this measurement step regardless of which graphics device is active for rendering. The warnings appear at the layout stage before ragg_png draws anything.

GDI only sees fonts installed system-wide in C:\Windows\Fonts. Per-user installs in AppData\Local\Microsoft\Windows\Fonts are invisible to GDI. Static {ggplot2} in the RStudio plot window uses the AGG backend set in Global Options -> General -> Graphics Backend. With {ragg} as the active device it intercepts grid's text measurement calls, so per-user fonts work there. animate() opens its own device per frame outside that context, and grid's measurement calls fall back to GDI which only sees system-wide fonts.

First, install the fonts so GDI can find them. Download IBM Plex Sans and EB Garamond from fonts.google.com, extract the zip files, select all .ttf files, right-click and install for all users. This puts them in C:\Windows\Fonts. Per-user install (the default double-click) is not sufficient.

Verify after installing and restarting R:

library(systemfonts)
system_fonts()[grep("EB Garamond|IBM Plex Sans", system_fonts()$family), "path"]
# paths should now show C:\Windows\Fonts\... not AppData\Local\... or not found

Since {ragg} handles fonts via {systemfonts}, {showtext} is not needed. Use the actual font family names instead of the "body" and "title" aliases that only existed in {showtext}'s registry:

library(ggplot2)
library(ggtext)
library(gganimate)
library(ragg)
showtext::showtext_auto(FALSE)  # disable showtext hook

windowsFonts(`IBM Plex Sans` = windowsFont("IBM Plex Sans"),
             `EB Garamond`   = windowsFont("EB Garamond"))

p <- ggplot(AftershocksInSequence,
            aes(x = TimeSincePrimaryEvent, y = magnitude, fill = fact_int_mag)) +
  geom_col(position = "identity") +
  labs(title    = "Title", subtitle = "{frame_time}", caption  = "Caption",
       x = "Time", y = "Magnitude", fill = "Magn.") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    text          = element_text(family = "IBM Plex Sans", color = "white"),
    axis.text     = element_text(color = "white", size = 6),
    axis.title    = element_text(size = 8),
    plot.title    = element_markdown(family = "EB Garamond"),
    plot.subtitle = element_markdown(family = "EB Garamond", 
                                     size = 6, lineheight = 1.1),
    plot.caption  = element_markdown(family = "EB Garamond", 
                                     size = 7, lineheight = 1.0)
  ) +
  transition_time(maxTime)

animate(p, nframes = 10, device = "ragg_png",
        renderer = gifski_renderer(loop = FALSE))

#> Inserting image 10 at 0.90s (100%)...
#> Encoding to gif... done!

windowsFonts() registers an alias with GDI so the font name resolves correctly for grid's text measurement calls. This only works after the fonts are installed system-wide.

Q: Is there a good online compiler for C quadruple precision float calculations, and what sample code can be used to test it? A:

Using on-line compiler with __float128

My search result is exactly like yours which also lands on Godbolt & OnlineGDB and just like you discovered, it require a linker flag -lquadmath.

For Godbolt, do these steps:

  1. On the left panel, type any valid code using __float128.
    • In the language menu, select C
  2. On the right panel, select x86-64 gcc 16.2 from the compiler list.
    • In "Compiler options..." box, enter -lquadmath
    • In "Output..." menu, select checkbox "Execute the code"
  3. At the bottom, click the "Output" button to show the output window.
  4. If the result is not there, click the spin-circle sign ("Clear cache & recompile") so it can rebuild again, the result should be displayed in output window, if the code is correct.

So, Godbolt can still use __float128 AFAIK. If you encountered a problem, one of the reasons could be that you chose a compiler other than GCC.

Off-line alternative

Compiling C code using GCC using quadruple precision float __float128 should not be a problem, just remember to include the option -lquadmath when building the binary executable. But GCC might not be always available on platforms other than Linux. The best alternative you can find is using the GNU MPFR Library. It's portable, supported by most major C compilers, and can have multiple-precision floating-point, not just quadruple.

As for the tests that you mentioned, MPFR its own source code is hosted here on gitlab and it comes with its own tests.

Q: ZkTeco custom payroll system development A:

The main difference is that ZKTeco Push SDK is designed for devices to push attendance/user data to your server, while the Standalone SDK generally communicates with the device directly over the network (typically TCP/IP) and lets your application control/query the device.

For your use case — a centralized custom payroll/attendance system with multiple ZKTeco devices — I would prefer the Push SDK, provided your MB60 firmware supports the required Push protocol.

With Push SDK, the architecture can be:

ZKTeco MB60 ─┐
ZKTeco MB60 ─┼──> Central API/Server ──> Database ──> Payroll System
ZKTeco MB60 ─┘

Each device can send attendance transactions to your centralized server. Your application can then maintain employees, attendance, shifts, overtime, payroll calculations, etc.

However, there is an important distinction: Push SDK is primarily for data synchronization/push communication, not necessarily a complete replacement for every device-management operation. If you need advanced operations such as creating/modifying users, enrolling fingerprints, deleting users, configuring the device, or synchronizing users across devices, you should verify that the specific MB60 firmware/protocol exposes those operations.

The Standalone SDK can be more appropriate when your application needs direct, programmatic control of each device:

Your Application
      │
      ├── TCP/IP ──> Device 1
      ├── TCP/IP ──> Device 2
      └── TCP/IP ──> Device 3

So, for a centralized payroll system, I'd generally recommend Push SDK for attendance collection + the appropriate ZKTeco device-management API/SDK for employee/device operations, rather than assuming one SDK handles everything.

Also check the exact MB60 firmware version and communication protocol supported by your particular device, because ZKTeco SDK compatibility can vary between models and firmware versions.
